paragraphs: Retrieval-augmented models make predictions using both an input and relevant information selected from a larger collection. This paper develops a statistical framework for understanding that combined system. It treats retrieval and prediction as distinct components: the retriever selects information using a data-dependent measure of relevance, while the predictor uses the selected information alongside the original input.

The authors propose a principled way to train both components together, connecting their method to existing training approaches. Joint training matters because the usefulness of retrieved information depends on how the predictor consumes it. Studying the components together provides a way to reason about that interaction rather than evaluating retrieval as an isolated preliminary step.

The theoretical contribution is a set of excess-risk bounds that distinguish the contributions of the retriever and predictor to overall performance. The authors also test their training methods and conclusions from the analysis on open-domain question answering. These experiments support the framework’s usefulness in a setting where finding relevant information is central to answering correctly.
icml-2024-a-statistical-framework-for-da.tldr: A statistical framework explains how retrievers and predictors jointly affect performance and provides a principled way to train them together.

paragraphs: Federated learning often requires a server to estimate the average of vectors held by many clients. Sending and processing these vectors efficiently makes distributed mean estimation an important part of the training system. This paper targets the computational work involved in preparing client messages and reconstructing their average at the server.

Earlier methods already achieve an optimal normalized mean squared error rate of O(1/n), where n is the number of clients. The authors improve the asymptotic complexity of encoding, decoding, or both while retaining that error guarantee. Their key methodological change is a new formulation of the problem that lets existing mathematical solvers design the quantization used to represent communicated values.

The resulting method, QUIC-FL, is evaluated across multiple datasets and training tasks. The authors report state-of-the-art accuracy alongside faster encoding and decoding than other distributed mean estimation methods. The contribution therefore addresses the computation surrounding communication: maintaining a strong accuracy guarantee while reducing the effort needed to turn client vectors into an estimated average.
icml-2024-accelerating-federated-learnin.tldr: QUIC-FL accelerates distributed mean estimation while retaining an optimal error rate and achieving strong federated-learning accuracy.

paragraphs: Image classifiers can perform extremely well on ordinary images yet struggle with small adversarial changes. Using CIFAR10, this paper studies how robustness depends on model size, dataset size, and synthetic-data quality. The authors develop scaling laws for adversarial training to understand both how efficiently existing methods use computation and how much improvement further scaling might deliver.

The analysis identifies substantial computational inefficiencies in prior methods. A more compute-efficient setup exceeds the previous best result with 20% fewer training FLOPs and 70% fewer inference FLOPs. Among the models trained, the strongest achieves 74% AutoAttack accuracy, a reported gain of 3%. These findings show that better allocation of computation can improve robustness without simply expanding resource use.

The scaling laws predict that robustness eventually plateaus near 90%, making large further gains through scaling impractical under that prediction. A small human study also estimates a plateau near 90% on attacks that fool the strongest model. The authors attribute this to some permitted perturbations producing images inconsistent with their original labels, linking the predicted ceiling to the evaluation’s label assumptions.
icml-2024-adversarial-robustness-limits-.tldr: Scaling laws improve adversarial-training efficiency while predicting a robustness ceiling linked to attacks that can invalidate original image labels.

paragraphs: Predicting how a physical system evolves often requires solving a partial differential equation repeatedly for different parameters or starting conditions. CoLoRA builds a reduced neural model for this task. It first pretrains a network for a given equation, then continuously changes a small, low-rank set of weights as time advances to predict new solution fields.

The central design choice is to approximate the solution locally in time. According to the authors, this allows the adapted weights to retain a small rank and reduces the number of training trajectories needed beforehand. The adaptation can follow data alone or use an equation-driven variational formulation. The latter provides Galerkin-optimal approximations, giving that version a stated mathematical optimality property.

The paper reports predictions that are orders of magnitude faster than classical methods, together with better accuracy and parameter efficiency than other neural approaches. Its practical appeal is the combination of rapid prediction at new physics parameters and initial conditions with limited offline training data. The small evolving adaptation is what connects the reduced model’s flexibility to its efficiency.
icml-2024-colora-continuous-low-rank-ada.tldr: CoLoRA continuously adapts low-rank neural weights to predict PDE solutions quickly from relatively few training trajectories.

paragraphs: D-Flow addresses how to steer an existing diffusion or flow-matching model toward a desired output without retraining a separate model for each task. Its control variable is the initial noise point that starts generation. The method differentiates through the generation process and adjusts that starting point so that the resulting output better satisfies the task’s objective.

The authors motivate this procedure with an observation about models trained using Gaussian probability paths. In that setting, differentiating through generation projects the gradient onto the data manifold, bringing the model’s learned prior into the optimization. This explains why optimizing the initial noise can use the structure learned by the generator while pursuing an external generation requirement.

The framework is tested on both linear and nonlinear controlled-generation problems. These include image and audio inverse problems and conditional molecule generation, with state-of-the-art performance reported across the evaluated problems. The result supports a common control mechanism across these tasks: modify the source noise through the generator’s gradients while using the pretrained generation process to shape the output.
icml-2024-d-flow-differentiating-through.tldr: D-Flow controls pretrained diffusion and flow-matching models by differentiating through generation to optimize their initial noise.

paragraphs: A learner may have only a small amount of labeled data from its target domain, with privacy constraints restricting its use. Public labeled data from a reasonably related domain can provide additional information. This paper studies how to combine these sources through supervised domain adaptation while protecting the private target data.

The authors introduce two algorithms with (epsilon, delta)-differential privacy guarantees, building on an optimization formulation with favorable learning guarantees. The first handles regression with linear predictors and solves a convex optimization problem. The second supports a broader class of losses that can be nonconvex, provided they satisfy Lipschitz and smoothness conditions. These conditions define the stated scope of the more general approach.

Although the main contribution is theoretical, experiments examine the cost of adding privacy. The nonprivate versions match state-of-the-art supervised adaptation performance. With larger target datasets or larger epsilon values, the private versions remain close to their nonprivate counterparts. The findings connect adaptation quality to both the amount of target information and the privacy setting, rather than claiming a uniform performance outcome.
icml-2024-differentially-private-domain-.tldr: Two theoretically supported algorithms adapt public labeled data to a private target domain under differential privacy.

paragraphs: Ordinary differential equations describe how a system changes over time, but their parameters must often be inferred from measurements. Even when gradients are available, this fitting problem can be difficult. Nonlinear dynamics can create many local minima, and strong sensitivity to initial conditions can make parameter optimization unreliable.

The paper introduces diffusion tempering, a regularization technique for probabilistic numerical integrators. Its central operation is to reduce an integrator’s noise parameter iteratively during gradient-based parameter fitting. This makes the noise setting part of the optimization procedure, rather than leaving it fixed throughout the search. The authors report that the resulting procedure converges more reliably to the true parameters.

The method is demonstrated on dynamical systems with different levels of complexity. The evaluation includes a Hodgkin–Huxley model with a practically relevant number of parameters, for which reliable parameter estimates are reported. These results support using the numerical integrator itself to improve parameter fitting: the contribution concerns how the differential equations are handled during optimization, addressing difficulties that differentiability alone does not resolve.
icml-2024-diffusion-tempering-improves-p.tldr: Diffusion tempering gradually reduces probabilistic-integrator noise to make gradient-based ODE parameter estimation more reliable.

paragraphs: Models can sometimes fit training noise and still predict well on new data, challenging a simple reading of the bias–variance tradeoff. This paper examines that behavior through kernel regression. The authors seek a unified theory covering nearly all common realistic settings, addressing what they describe as restrictive assumptions or narrow scope in much earlier work.

Their main results upper-bound excess risk, measuring how far prediction performance is from the relevant optimal reference. Applied to common kernels, the bounds imply benign overfitting in high input dimensions, nearly tempered overfitting in fixed dimensions, and explicit convergence rates when regularization is used. The distinctions matter: the theory does not assign the same overfitting behavior to every dimensional setting.

The analysis relies on new relative perturbation bounds for kernel-matrix eigenvalues. These reveal a self-regularization effect in which a heavy tail in the kernel’s eigendecomposition can implicitly support good generalization. As an additional consequence, the authors obtain time-dependent bounds for neural networks trained in the kernel regime, extending the analysis to that particular neural-network setting.
icml-2024-generalization-in-kernel-regre.tldr: A unified kernel-regression analysis links generalization and overfitting behavior to dimension, regularization, and the kernel’s eigenvalue structure.

paragraphs: A graph neural network receives connections between data points, but those connections do not always help predict the desired outcome. Although the model can represent solutions that ignore the graph, this paper asks whether training actually finds them. The authors show a tendency to use graph structure even when ignoring it would produce a better solution.

The theoretical analysis studies the implicit bias of gradient descent. When the true target function does not depend on the graph, the learned solution is still not guaranteed to ignore graph structure, even with unlimited data. This separates the model’s representational ability from its training behavior: having a suitable solution available does not ensure that optimization selects it.

The authors also examine how the graph distribution affects this problem. Regular graphs are more resistant to the observed overfitting, and the paper proves an extrapolation guarantee within the family of regular graphs for gradient-descent learning. Guided by the theoretical and empirical findings, experiments on real data demonstrate that using regular graphs can reduce graph overfitting and improve performance.
icml-2024-graph-neural-networks-use-grap.tldr: Gradient descent can make GNNs rely on unhelpful graph structure, while regular graphs offer theoretical and empirical ways to reduce this behavior.

paragraphs: Detecting an unusual node in a graph requires considering its relationships with other nodes. This paper introduces TopoOOD, an approach to out-of-distribution detection that incorporates graph topology and neighborhood context. The goal is to identify node instances that differ from the distribution treated as familiar by the model.

The work also changes how graph detectors are evaluated. The authors construct benchmarks that separate familiar and unfamiliar data according to distinct topological distributions. This explicitly tests distribution shifts involving structural information. Such evaluation matters because a detector’s ability to recognize unfamiliar graph relationships is part of its intended job, and the benchmark makes that ability a direct object of study.

Across multiple datasets, TopoOOD is reported to be competitive with existing state-of-the-art methods. The abstract reports improvements of up to 15% in AUROC and reductions of up to 50% in false-positive rate. These are maximum reported gains, rather than uniform improvements across every evaluation. Together, the method and benchmarks put neighborhood structure at the center of both graph anomaly detection and its assessment.
icml-2024-graph-out-of-distribution-dete.tldr: TopoOOD uses graph structure and neighborhood context to detect unfamiliar nodes, with new benchmarks explicitly testing structural distribution shifts.

paragraphs: Explaining a single prediction and explaining a model’s behavior across inputs are different computational tasks. This paper gives those local and global perspectives a formal treatment using computational complexity theory. The aim is to determine how difficult particular explanation problems are, moving beyond informal judgments about which model types seem interpretable.

The authors first prove a duality between local and global explanations and establish uniqueness for certain forms of global explanation. They then use these results to analyze linear models, decision trees, and neural networks. These model families provide contrasting cases for examining whether an explanation task becomes easier or harder when its scope changes.

For selecting sufficient subsets, the answer depends on the model family. Under standard complexity assumptions such as P not equaling NP, the global task is harder than the local task for linear models. For decision trees and neural networks, the ordering reverses. This shows that the computational difficulty of explanation depends jointly on the model, the explanation form, and whether the requested explanation is local or global.
icml-2024-local-vs-global-interpretabili.tldr: The relative difficulty of local and global explanations reverses across model families for the sufficient-subset task studied.

paragraphs: Individual fairness asks a learner to treat similar people similarly while making accurate predictions. This paper studies that objective in online learning, where decisions arrive sequentially and human auditors report fairness violations. The authors extend earlier frameworks to combine feedback from any number of auditors through a broad class of monotone aggregation functions, which they also characterize mathematically.

Within this framework, they provide an oracle-efficient algorithm whose regret and number of fairness violations are both bounded by O(T^(3/4)) over T rounds. Regret tracks the learner’s cumulative predictive shortfall against its comparison standard. Bounding it alongside violations means the analysis addresses predictive performance and fairness within the same sequential process.

The paper also considers selective feedback, where labels become available only for individuals given positive predictions. In that setting, both quantities receive O(T^(5/6)) bounds. The algorithms improve the best known bounds for oracle-efficient methods in their respective settings. They also substantially reduce calls to an offline optimization oracle compared with earlier algorithms that required T such calls in every round.
icml-2024-monotone-individual-fairness-2.tldr: New online-learning algorithms combine multiple auditors’ fairness feedback while improving regret, violation bounds, and optimization-oracle efficiency.

paragraphs: Conventional diffusion models commonly restrict how they transform the data distribution to linear transformations. Neural Diffusion Models expand this design space by learning nonlinear transformations that vary with time. The motivation is that a more flexible transformation family can make the reverse generation process easier and tighten the variational approximation used to assess likelihood.

The paper develops a way to optimize these models through a variational bound without simulation during that optimization. It also derives a continuous-time formulation. This allows inference to use existing numerical solvers for ordinary and stochastic differential equations, connecting the generalized model to established tools for carrying out the generation process.

Experiments cover MNIST, CIFAR-10, downsampled ImageNet, and CelebA-HQ. The authors report better likelihoods than conventional diffusion models, including state-of-the-art likelihood results on ImageNet and CelebA-HQ, along with high-quality samples. The contribution is therefore both a broader mathematical model and an implementable training and inference framework, with the evaluated likelihood gains supporting the value of learning more flexible transformations.
icml-2024-neural-diffusion-models-f06ccb.tldr: Neural Diffusion Models learn time-dependent nonlinear transformations and improve likelihoods across image-generation benchmarks.

paragraphs: The distributional simplicity bias proposes that neural networks first learn lower-order statistics of their training data and later learn more complex correlations. This paper supplies new evidence for that progression. It examines how networks behave on maximum-entropy distributions constructed to share low-order statistics with the training set.

Early in training, networks perform well on these matched distributions, but later lose that ability. This pattern supports the idea that their initial predictions depend on simpler statistical features before shifting toward information those distributions do not preserve. The authors also extend the analysis to discrete data by proving an equivalence between token n-gram frequencies and moments of embedding vectors, and they find empirical evidence of the bias in language models.

A further experiment uses optimal transport to change one class’s low-order statistics so they match those of another class. Early-training networks then treat the edited examples as belonging to the target class. This intervention strengthens the evidence that low-order statistics influence early predictions, complementing the observed changes in generalization over training.
icml-2024-neural-networks-learn-statisti.tldr: Statistical matching and targeted data edits support the view that networks learn simpler distributional features before higher-order correlations.

paragraphs: Non-clairvoyant scheduling concerns decisions made without knowing job sizes in advance. Predictions can help, but obtaining them may be costly or impossible for some jobs. This paper studies a restricted-information setting in which the scheduling algorithm receives size predictions for only B of its n jobs, rather than assuming predictions are available throughout the workload.

The authors first analyze perfect predictions for that limited subset. They establish lower bounds and algorithms that are near-optimal in this setting. This separates the consequences of incomplete prediction coverage from the consequences of inaccurate predictions: even correct information is available for only part of the scheduling problem.

They then introduce a learning-augmented algorithm with robustness, consistency, and smoothness guarantees. These criteria concern protection when predictions are poor, performance when they are accurate, and how performance changes as prediction quality worsens. The analysis reveals a tradeoff between consistency and smoothness when prediction coverage is restricted. The result shows that designing for partial access requires balancing distinct benefits of prediction, beyond merely accounting for prediction errors.
icml-2024-non-clairvoyant-scheduling-wit.tldr: Scheduling with predictions for only some jobs admits near-optimal guarantees and exposes a tradeoff between consistency and smoothness.

paragraphs: Editing a text-to-image model efficiently requires identifying which internal layers influence the visual attribute to be changed. Earlier causal-tracing work found localized knowledge in early Stable Diffusion variants, but this paper reports that the same approach fails to pinpoint localized knowledge in newer models such as SD-XL and DeepFloyd. This creates a practical obstacle for localization-based editing.

The authors introduce mechanistic localization, focusing on layers’ direct effects on generated outputs. Their method, LocoGen, intervenes in the UNet’s cross-attention layers to identify where attributes such as style, objects, and facts can be controlled. Under this approach, knowledge about these attributes can be localized to a small fraction of UNet layers.

The paper then uses LocoEdit, a fast closed-form editing method, across popular open-source text-to-image models including SD-XL. It also explores editing at the level of individual neurons. The contribution links localization to an actionable editing mechanism and offers an account of why localization-based edits succeed or fail, even when an earlier tracing procedure does not identify a clear location.
icml-2024-on-mechanistic-knowledge-local.tldr: LocoGen identifies layers that directly control visual attributes, enabling fast closed-form edits in text-to-image models including SD-XL.

paragraphs: Image keypoints provide identifiable locations that support tasks such as robotics and image retrieval. This paper addresses scale dependence and limited flexibility in existing learning-based detectors. It introduces MorseDet, a detector built around mathematical tools from topology, with the aim of giving feature detection a principled foundation.

The approach combines Morse theory and persistent homology. Its central training contribution is a new loss function based on a recently introduced notion of a subgradient for persistent homology. This supplies a route for incorporating the topological formulation into learning. The loss therefore connects the mathematical description of image features to the process used to train the detector.

The authors describe MorseDet as the first topology-based learning model for feature detection and report competitive keypoint repeatability. Repeatability concerns whether a detector can identify corresponding keypoints consistently, making it directly relevant to their usefulness. The stated contribution combines that competitive performance with a theoretically grounded approach to detection; the abstract does not claim that MorseDet universally outperforms existing detectors.
icml-2024-scale-free-image-keypoints-usi.tldr: MorseDet trains an image-keypoint detector using a persistent-homology loss and achieves competitive repeatability.

paragraphs: Sequential disentanglement aims to separate what stays constant in a sequence from what changes over time. A representation should contain one static factor and a series of dynamic factors. Existing methods often infer both from the entire sequence, but information can leak between them: dynamic codes may retain static content, or static codes may contain changing information.

This paper introduces a simpler architecture that extracts static information from a single sequence element and uses a subtraction-based inductive bias to mitigate leakage. Rather than relying primarily on smaller dynamic representations or additional loss terms, it builds a preference for separation into the architecture. The resulting variational framework requires fewer loss terms, hyperparameters, and data augmentations.

The authors evaluate the method on general time series, video, and audio benchmarks. They report results beyond the state of the art on generation and prediction tasks compared with several strong baselines. The findings support the architectural choice as a way to improve usable sequence representations while simplifying training, with the claimed benefit being reduced information leakage rather than a guarantee of perfect separation.
icml-2024-sequential-disentanglement-by-.tldr: A single-element static representation and subtraction-based architecture reduce information leakage while improving sequence generation and prediction.

paragraphs: Higher-order input statistics can contain useful features, but extracting them with stochastic gradient descent can be expensive. In the tensor-PCA problem described by the authors, recovering one direction from an order-p statistic of d-dimensional data requires a number of samples growing as d^(p−1). This creates a puzzle about how networks can efficiently learn information carried by complex correlations.

The paper identifies correlations between latent variables as a mechanism that can accelerate learning. When latent variables connect directions represented in different input cumulants, learning higher-order information becomes faster. The contribution is to show how relationships among the hidden sources of the data can change the difficulty suggested by studying a higher-order statistic in isolation.

The authors derive nearly sharp sample thresholds for a single neuron trained with online SGD from a random initialization in high dimensions. Simulations with two-layer networks confirm the analytical effect. These findings establish a mechanism for hierarchical learning in the studied setting: correlations across latent variables can help networks reach statistically more complex features with fewer samples.
icml-2024-sliding-down-the-stairs-how-co.tldr: Correlations between latent variables can accelerate SGD’s recovery of features encoded in higher-order input statistics.

paragraphs: Fairness assessment for continuous risk scores needs to describe the size of disparities between groups, not just identify that some disparity exists. This paper proposes standardized fairness measures with an interpretation based on Wasserstein distance. The emphasis is on making differences in score distributions both computable and understandable.

Standardization is central to the intended use. The authors design the measures to support comparisons across models, datasets, and time points, so that an assessment can address how the strength of a disparity differs between settings. They also derive a connection between existing families of score-based fairness measures, placing the proposed quantities within a broader mathematical account of how these assessments relate.

The authors report that their measures outperform ROC-based fairness measures in explicitness and in detecting significant biases that the ROC-based measures miss. The claimed improvement concerns the ability to quantify and interpret group disparities in continuous scores. This makes the work a contribution to fairness measurement: it provides a clearer way to characterize observed differences and compare their magnitude across evaluated systems.
icml-2024-standardized-interpretable-fai.tldr: Standardized Wasserstein-based fairness measures quantify group disparities in continuous scores, including biases missed by ROC-based measures.

paragraphs: Masked image modeling learns from unlabeled images by predicting missing content. That task mixes two demands: recognizing what belongs in the image and locating it precisely. The visible content may support a plausible semantic prediction without determining its exact position, creating uncertainty that a model’s training should account for.

The paper introduces stochastic positional embeddings, called StoP, to represent that uncertainty. Instead of conditioning only on fixed masked-token positions, the model receives positions sampled from a Gaussian distribution. The authors show that this reduces overfitting to location features and encourages representations that remain useful when location is uncertain. The change directly targets the positional information supplied during masked-image learning.

StoP improves downstream performance on a variety of tasks in the reported experiments. Examples include a reported 1.7% improvement in ImageNet linear probing with ViT-B and 2.5% with ViT-H using 1% of the data. These results support treating location uncertainty as part of representation learning, with benefits measured through the usefulness of the resulting features on downstream tasks.
icml-2024-stochastic-positional-embeddin.tldr: Sampling masked-token positions from a Gaussian distribution reduces location overfitting and improves masked-image representations.

paragraphs: Subgraph neural networks and graph transformers offer different ingredients for learning from graph structure. Subgraph methods provide expressive message passing and aggregation, while transformers contribute attention and positional information. Subgraphormer brings these ingredients together through a mathematical connection that gives the combined architecture a common structural basis.

The authors show that subgraph GNNs can be formulated as message-passing networks operating on a product of a graph with itself. They use this formulation to design attention around the connectivity of the product graph. They also derive an efficient positional encoding for subgraph GNNs by treating it as a positional encoding problem on that same product graph.

This construction matters because the attention mechanism and positional information both arise from the structure used to express subgraph computation. The architecture consequently links the two research directions through a shared formulation. Experiments report significant performance improvements over both subgraph GNNs and graph transformers across a wide range of datasets, supporting the usefulness of the integrated design in the evaluated settings.
icml-2024-subgraphormer-unifying-subgrap.tldr: Subgraphormer uses graph products to combine subgraph message passing with structurally grounded attention and positional encodings.

paragraphs: Language models can reproduce memorized training passages, creating privacy and related copyright concerns. Unlearning seeks to remove such memorized material while preserving useful model capabilities. This paper argues that the removal process should account for how strongly each individual sequence is memorized, rather than applying the same treatment across the entire set to be forgotten.

The authors contribute a measure of unlearning quality and an adversarial attack showing privacy failures in state-of-the-art algorithms that lack this sequence-specific perspective. They also introduce two unlearning methods, one based on gradient ascent and the other on task arithmetic. Both incorporate the central idea that different sequences warrant different unlearning treatment.

An extensive evaluation across natural-language tasks examines the resulting balance between forgetting and utility. It compares solutions at different model capacities and forget-set sizes, identifies the best options within those settings, and quantifies gains from the proposed approaches. The findings make the choice of unlearning method sensitive to both the model and the material being removed, while the attack provides a direct test of whether apparent forgetting withstands adversarial probing.
icml-2024-to-each-textual-sequence-its-o.tldr: Sequence-specific unlearning accounts for memorization strength and improves the evaluated tradeoffs between forgetting, privacy, and model utility.

paragraphs: Estimating uncertainty in a single network pass requires features that distinguish when predictions are reliable. Some approaches preserve distances between examples as information moves through the network. This paper studies a tension in that strategy: preserving those distances can interfere with the information compression needed to learn the prediction task.

The theoretical and empirical analysis finds that preserving output features helps when those features contribute to learning the label distribution, but works against learning otherwise. The authors propose TULIP, which draws on intermediate representations before later layers collapse information. They call this mechanism transitional feature preservation, using layered intermediate predictions to retain information relevant to uncertainty.

This design makes intermediate stages useful for uncertainty estimation without requiring every useful distinction to survive in the final representation. Experiments show that TULIP matches or exceeds current single-pass methods on standard benchmarks. The reported evaluation also covers class imbalances, complex architectures, and medical modalities, settings where existing methods are less reliable. The findings support intermediate feature extraction as a practical response to the identified compression conflict.
icml-2024-transitional-uncertainty-with-.tldr: TULIP uses intermediate network predictions to preserve uncertainty information before later layers compress it.

paragraphs: Brain-activity representations can lose useful information when they focus only on summarized voxel activity or only on connections between larger brain regions. The first approach can miss temporal dynamics, while the second can omit voxel-level signals. BrainMixer brings voxel time series and functional connectivity into one unsupervised framework for learning voxel-level representations.

The architecture uses two encoders built from multilayer perceptrons to learn signal dynamics and functional correlations together. For voxel activity, a dynamic attention mechanism combines information across time and voxels. For connectivity, the method forms temporal graph patches and encodes each patch by combining node features through adaptive temporal pooling. These components address the two information sources within the same learning framework.

Experiments report that BrainMixer outperforms 14 baselines across different downstream tasks and setups. The findings support combining fine-grained temporal activity with connectivity structure when learning brain representations without supervision. The paper positions this representation learning as a step toward understanding cognition and neurological disorders, while the stated experimental result concerns performance on the evaluated downstream tasks.
icml-2024-unsupervised-representation-le.tldr: BrainMixer jointly learns voxel dynamics and functional connectivity, outperforming 14 baselines across evaluated downstream tasks and setups.
